Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

[LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm payload dropped under node_modules (router_init.js / tanstack_runner.js / known SHA256) Delivery High
Hunts the file-drop stage of the TeamPCP Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm (May 2026 wave) where compromised @tanstack / @squawk / @uipath / @tallyui / @mistralai / @beproduct / @draftauth / @draftlab tarballs unpack three named JavaScript payloads (router_init.js, router_runtime.js, tanstack_runner.js) into node_modules — or any file matching the two confirmed SHA256s. Triggers on developer workstations and CI runners during `npm install` / `pnpm install` / `yarn install` / `bun install`. Rationale: router_init.js, router_runtime.js and tanstack_runner.js are campaign-unique filenames called out in the Aikido article and corroborated by Socket, StepSecurity, Snyk and Wiz; the two SHA256s are directly from the article's IOC table. File-drop into node_modules combined with a node/npm/bun/pnpm/yarn initiator narrows scope to dependency-install activity, virtually eliminating FPs. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://snyk.io/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-strikes-again-tanstack-more-npm-packages-compromised • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/mini-shai-hulud-worm-compromises.html

[LLM] Bun spawned with tanstack_runner.js via npm prepare lifecycle (Mini Shai-Hulud) Installation High
Catches the execution stage of the Mini Shai-Hulud worm: `bun run tanstack_runner.js && exit 1` invoked from the @tanstack/setup optional-dependency prepare hook during `npm install`. The parent is node/npm/pnpm/yarn and the commandline references either tanstack_runner.js, @tanstack/setup, or the campaign's git commit hash 79ac49eedf774dd4b0cfa308722bc463cfe5885c. Rationale: The article explicitly documents `bun run tanstack_runner.js && exit 1` as the prepare-hook execution and pins the trigger to the @tanstack/setup Git dependency at commit 79ac49eedf774dd4b0cfa308722bc463cfe5885c — all three strings are uniquely tied to this campaign. Bun is rarely a child of node/npm in normal CI outside of TanStack ecosystems, and any match including the commit hash is essentially zero-FP. Cross-checked against Socket and StepSecurity write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/tanstack-router-packages-hit-by-coordinated-supply-chain-attack/

   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "79ac49eedf774dd4b0cfa308722bc463cfe5885c"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.cmd","npm","pnpm.cmd","pnpm","yarn.cmd","yarn","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash")

[LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud persistence to ~/.claude/hooks and .vscode/tasks.json by node/npm/bun Installation High
Catches the worm's developer-workstation persistence stage: after credential theft, the Mini Shai-Hulud payload writes copies of itself into Claude Code's hook directory (`~/.claude/hooks/`) and the VS Code task runner (`.vscode/tasks.json`) so it re-executes across reboots and editor relaunches. Initiator is a JavaScript runtime (node/npm/bun/pnpm/yarn), which is highly unusual for these specific paths. Rationale: The .claude/hooks and .vscode/tasks.json persistence is not in the Aikido article body but is confirmed by Socket and StepSecurity write-ups of the same May 2026 wave — both name these exact paths as the worm's mechanism to survive across reboots and extend infection from CI into developer workstations. A JavaScript runtime writing into either path is anomalous (these are normally edited by humans / the IDE itself), making this a high-fidelity pivot. Drop this UC if Claude Code is not in use anywhere in the estate. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem

   or (FileName =~ "tasks.json" and (FolderPath has @"\.vscode" or FolderPath has "/.vscode"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.cmd","npm","bun.exe","bun","pnpm.cmd","pnpm","yarn.cmd","yarn")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (TargetFilePath has @"\.claude\hooks" or TargetFilePath has "/.claude/hooks")
   or (TargetFileName =~ "tasks.json" and (TargetFilePath has @"\.vscode" or TargetFilePath has "/.vscode"))
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","bun","pnpm","yarn")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-45321")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-45321")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12ed9a3c1f73617aefdb740480695c04405d7b4b", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79", "833fd59ebe66a4449982c6d18db656b4", "b82e54923f7e440664d2d75bd31588ca") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12ed9a3c1f73617aefdb740480695c04405d7b4b", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79", "833fd59ebe66a4449982c6d18db656b4", "b82e54923f7e440664d2d75bd31588ca") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12ed9a3c1f73617aefdb740480695c04405d7b4b", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79", "833fd59ebe66a4449982c6d18db656b4", "b82e54923f7e440664d2d75bd31588ca")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12ed9a3c1f73617aefdb740480695c04405d7b4b", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79", "833fd59ebe66a4449982c6d18db656b4", "b82e54923f7e440664d2d75bd31588ca") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12ed9a3c1f73617aefdb740480695c04405d7b4b", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79", "833fd59ebe66a4449982c6d18db656b4", "b82e54923f7e440664d2d75bd31588ca") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12ed9a3c1f73617aefdb740480695c04405d7b4b", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79", "833fd59ebe66a4449982c6d18db656b4", "b82e54923f7e440664d2d75bd31588ca")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12ed9a3c1f73617aefdb740480695c04405d7b4b", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79", "833fd59ebe66a4449982c6d18db656b4", "b82e54923f7e440664d2d75bd31588ca"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2022-26923 exploitation via update6.exe binary execution · [LLM] AD CS certificate request with ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT flag (ESC1) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Inside AD CS Escalation: Unpacking Advanced Misuse Techniques and Tools
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] AD CS attacker tooling execution: Certify, Certipy, Whisker process indicators · [LLM] Shadow Credentials: msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute modification · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PKINIT Kerberos TGT request via certificate authentication anomaly · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
[LLM] CVE-2022-26923 exploitation via update6.exe binary execution Exploitation High
Detects execution of the update6.exe binary observed in Rapid7-reported AD CS social-engineering campaigns exploiting CVE-2022-26923. The binary requests certificates from AD CS to escalate privileges via dNSHostName attribute manipulation. Rationale: Article explicitly names update6.exe as the dropper observed in Rapid7's August 2024 campaign exploiting CVE-2022-26923. Cross-referenced with Rapid7 advisory and Microsoft MSRC CVE-2022-26923 page describing certificate-based privilege escalation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2024/08/ • https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2022-26923 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1649/
ATT&CKT1068 T1649
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "update6.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "update6.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\update6.exe" or CommandLine has "update6.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Suspicious update6.exe Execution (CVE-2022-26923)
id: 7c2b3a4d-1e5f-4a6b-9c8d-0e1f2a3b4c5d
description: Detects execution of update6.exe binary used in known CVE-2022-26923 exploitation campaigns against AD CS

tags:

  category: process_creation
  product: windows

| ImageFileName=/\\update6\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/update6\.exe/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="update6.exe" OR Processes.process=*update6.exe*) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
[LLM] AD CS attacker tooling execution: Certify, Certipy, Whisker process indicators Installation High
Detects execution of public AD CS exploitation tools (Certify.exe, certipy, Whisker.exe, pyWhisker) named in the article as the standard attacker toolkit for certificate template abuse and shadow-credential attacks. Rationale: Article's Table 2 explicitly enumerates Certify, Certipy, Whisker, and pyWhisker as the attacker toolkit. CLI strings 'find -vulnerable', 'shadow auto', 'req -ca' are documented command syntax in the public GitHub repos for these tools. Cross-referenced with MITRE ATT&CK T1649 and the public Certipy/Certify GitHub project docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/ly4k/Certipy • https://github.com/GhostPack/Certify • https://github.com/eladshamir/Whisker • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1649/
ATT&CKT1649 T1098
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("Certify.exe","certipy.exe","Whisker.exe","pywhisker.exe","certipy-ad.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("certipy ","Certify.exe ","pywhisker ","Whisker.exe ","find -vulnerable","req -ca ","req /ca:","shadow auto","shadow add","shadow list","-template ","/template:","-asreproast","-kerberoast")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\Certify.exe","\\certipy.exe","\\Whisker.exe","\\pywhisker.exe","\\certipy-ad.exe")
   or CommandLine has_any ("certipy ","Certify.exe ","pywhisker ","Whisker.exe ","find -vulnerable","req -ca ","req /ca:","shadow auto","shadow add","shadow list")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

[LLM] Shadow Credentials: msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute modification Installation High
Detects modification of the msDS-KeyCredentialLink LDAP attribute, the core persistence technique used by Whisker/pyWhisker to attach an attacker-controlled key to a target account for PKINIT-based authentication. This is the canonical shadow-credentials persistence signal. Rationale: Article's Table 2 names Whisker (C#) and pyWhisker (Python) specifically as tools that 'manipulate the msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute.' This attribute change on a privileged account is the canonical shadow-credentials persistence signal — corroborated with SpecterOps's seminal write-up on Key Trust abuse and the Whisker GitHub repository. Cross-checked against: • https://posts.specterops.io/shadow-credentials-abusing-key-trust-account-mapping-for-takeover-8ee1a53566ec • https://github.com/eladshamir/Whisker • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/001/
ATT&CKT1098.001 T1556
Data sourcesChange.Account_Management
IdentityQueryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Query has "msDS-KeyCredentialLink" or QueryTarget has "msDS-KeyCredentialLink"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, AccountName, AccountDomain, AccountUpn, DeviceName, IPAddress, Query, QueryTarget, QueryType, Protocol, Application
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 5136
| where EventData has "msDS-KeyCredentialLink"

[LLM] PKINIT Kerberos TGT request via certificate authentication anomaly Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects Kerberos pre-authentication (EID 4768) using PKINIT/certificate where the certificate subject does not match the requesting account — the core behavioural signal of CVE-2022-26923 exploitation and certificate-based account impersonation highlighted in the Unit 42 article. Rationale: Article's Phase 4 explicitly calls out 'Using certificates or keys with public key cryptography for initial authentication (PKINIT) to request Kerberos tickets and impersonate privileged users.' EID 4768 with CertSerialNumber/CertIssuerName/CertThumbprint populated (parsed from EventData XML) is the on-the-wire signature of PKINIT auth — Microsoft documents these fields as part of the 4768 audit event. Cross-referenced with Microsoft MSRC CVE-2022-26923 and MITRE T1649. Cross-checked against: • https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2022-26923 • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4768 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1649/
ATT&CKT1558.003 T1649 T1550
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
IdentityLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Protocol == "Kerberos"
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where AdditionalFields has_any ("PKINIT","Certificate","SmartCard")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Count = count(), Devices = make_set(DeviceName), IPs = make_set(IPAddress) by AccountName, AccountDomain, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Count > 0
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4768
| extend CertIssuerName = tostring(extract(@"<Data Name=\"CertIssuerName\">([^<]+)<", 1, EventData))
| extend CertSerialNumber = tostring(extract(@"<Data Name=\"CertSerialNumber\">([^<]+)<", 1, EventData))
| extend CertThumbprint = tostring(extract(@"<Data Name=\"CertThumbprint\">([^<]+)<", 1, EventData))
| where isnotempty(CertSerialNumber) or isnotempty(CertThumbprint)
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$"
| summarize TGTCount = count(), Issuers = make_set(CertIssuerName), Serials = make_set(CertSerialNumber), SourceIPs = make_set(IpAddress) by TargetUserName, TargetDomainName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4768 (@EventData:*CertSerialNumber* OR @EventData:*CertIssuerName* OR @EventData:*PKINIT*) -@TargetUserName:*$
#event_simpleName=UserLogon
| AuthenticationPackage=/Kerberos/i
| LogonType=2 OR LogonType=3 OR LogonType=10
| (RawEventData=/PKINIT/i OR RawEventData=/CertSerialNumber/i OR RawEventData=/SmartCard/i)
| NOT UserName=/\$$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())

[LLM] AD CS certificate request with ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT flag (ESC1) Exploitation Medium
Detects ESC1-style certificate requests where the requester supplies an arbitrary subject in the Certificate Signing Request — the exact misconfiguration the article describes attackers abusing to mint authentication certificates for high-privilege accounts they don't control. Rationale: Article explicitly calls out the ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT template flag ('Supply in the request' option) as the key misconfiguration enabling ESC1. EIDs 4886/4887/4888 on AD CS servers carry the Requester and the Attributes blob (parsed from EventData XML) which includes the requested SubjectAltName UPN — a mismatch between Requester and SAN UPN is the textbook ESC1 signal documented by SpecterOps's Certified Pre-Owned research. Cross-checked against: • https://posts.specterops.io/certified-pre-owned-d95910965cd2 • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-fs/troubleshooting/ad-fs-tshoot-logging • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1649/
ATT&CKT1649 T1078.002
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("CertificateRequest","CertificateIssued")
   or AdditionalFields has_any ("ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT","CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain, ActionType, AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4886, 4887, 4888)
| extend Requester = tostring(extract(@"<Data Name=\"Requester\">([^<]+)<", 1, EventData))
| extend Attributes = tostring(extract(@"<Data Name=\"Attributes\">([^<]+)<", 1, EventData))
| extend TemplateName = tostring(extract(@"<Data Name=\"TemplateName\">([^<]+)<", 1, EventData))
| extend SubjectAltName = tostring(extract(@"san:[^<]*upn=([^&<]+)", 1, Attributes))
| where isnotempty(SubjectAltName) and isnotempty(Requester)
| extend RequesterUser = tolower(tostring(split(Requester, "\\")[1]))
| extend SANUser = tolower(tostring(split(SubjectAltName, "@")[0]))
| where RequesterUser != SANUser
| where Requester !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Requester, RequesterUser, SubjectAltName, SANUser, TemplateName, Attributes, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.security (@EventID:4886 OR @EventID:4887 OR @EventID:4888) (@EventData:*upn=* OR @EventData:*CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT* OR @Attributes:*SubjectAltName*) -@SubjectUserName:*$
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (CommandLine=/certreq\.exe.*-attrib/i OR CommandLine=/certipy.*req/i OR CommandLine=/Certify\.exe\s+request/i OR CommandLine=/upn=.*@/i)
| ParentBaseFileName!=/services\.exe/i
| NOT UserName=/\$$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where (All_Changes.signature_id=4886 OR All_Changes.signature_id=4887) by All_Changes.dest All_Changes.user All_Changes.object All_Changes.object_attrs All_Changes.action | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where (All_Changes.signature_id=4886 OR All_Changes.signature_id=4887) by All_Changes.dest All_Changes.user All_Changes.object All_Changes.object_attrs All_Changes.action | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2022-26923")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2022-26923")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Node.js spawning OS recon/shell binaries (post-exploit of SandboxJS escape CVE-2026-43898) Exploitation High
Hunts node.exe (the host process embedding @nyariv/sandboxjs <= 0.9.5) spawning shell or built-in recon binaries — the visible footprint of a Function.caller→LispType.Call escape that lands a child_process.execSync('whoami') style RCE on the host. Node legitimately almost never spawns cmd/whoami/net/ipconfig/hostname/wmic/powershell, so a single hit on a SandboxJS-using service is high-fidelity. Rationale: The article's PoC ends in process.getBuiltinModule('child_process').execSync('whoami').toString() — the on-host artifact is a node.exe parent spawning whoami.exe (or any equivalent shell/recon LOLBin once the attacker pivots from the canary). Filters exclude legitimate npm/yarn/node-gyp/electron build flows that legitimately fork shells from node. CVE source: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8f2-4f4f-5jqw. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8f2-4f4f-5jqw • https://github.com/nyariv/SandboxJS/blob/1e6785658c94f5f2fb8e4a02cfcf1e7821b8be7f/src/executor/ops/call.ts • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-43898
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1082 T1033
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","ipconfig.exe","hostname.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe","wmic.exe","reg.exe","sh.exe","bash.exe")
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","npm-cli.js","yarn.js","\\node_modules\\.bin\\","electron-builder"))
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","yarn install","node-gyp configure"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessId, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| extend NewProcLeaf = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where NewProcLeaf in ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","ipconfig.exe","hostname.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe","wmic.exe","reg.exe","sh.exe","bash.exe")
| where not (CommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","npm-cli.js","yarn.js","node_modules\\.bin","electron-builder","npm install","yarn install"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, AccountName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, NewProcessId, ProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] pgAdmin 4 server-mode hosts vulnerable to CVE-2026-7813 (auth bypass + passexec_cmd RCE pre-9.15) Reconnaissance High
Inventories Windows/Linux endpoints running pgAdmin 4 builds below 9.15, which expose the Server Groups / Shared Servers / Background Process / Debugger authorization bypass and the writable passexec_cmd RCE described in GHSA-h2x2-q2mc-24gw. Prioritises internet-reachable server-mode deployments where authenticated-user object-ID guessing is exploitable. Rationale: Locks onto the exact fixed-version line in the advisory ("affects pgAdmin 4: before 9.15") plus the assigned CveId. The version-regex fallback catches hosts whose vendor TVM KB hasn't published the CVE yet but whose installed pgAdmin build is pre-9.15. Datadog/Falcon left blank — FDR and Datadog Cloud SIEM do not ship vulnerability-inventory data by default; this detection is intentionally an EDR/TVM pivot. Sigma omitted because vuln-inventory is not single-event-shape. [LLM] pgAdmin 4 server process spawning shell/interpreter — passexec_cmd RCE (CVE-2026-7813) Exploitation High
Catches the privilege-escalation primitive from CVE-2026-7813: a non-owner who writes the Shared Server's passexec_cmd field causes pgAdmin to execute that shell command in the owner's process context the next time the connection is established. The signal is pgAdmin4.exe / the gunicorn|uwsgi|python interpreter hosting pgAdmin4.py spawning cmd / powershell / pwsh / bash / sh / wscript / cscript / mshta — a child shape pgAdmin's normal libpq workflow never produces. Rationale: Locks onto the exact privilege-escalation primitive named in GHSA-h2x2-q2mc-24gw: writable passexec_cmd is a shell command that pgAdmin invokes when establishing a connection, so when exploited it manifests as the pgAdmin process tree branching into a shell/interpreter — a child shape pgAdmin's normal libpq / pg_dump / pg_restore flow never produces. The pg_dump/pg_restore/psql exclusion preserves precision for the backup-wizard FP path. Cross-checked against SecurityOnline (https://securityonline.info/pgadmin-4-critical-vulnerabilities-rce-authorization-bypass-v9-15/) and the upstream PostgreSQL 9.15 release note confirming this is the writable-field RCE chain (not a separate code-injection bug). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h2x2-q2mc-24gw • https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-7813 • https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/pgadmin-4-v915-released-3295/ • https://securityonline.info/pgadmin-4-critical-vulnerabilities-rce-authorization-bypass-v9-15/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/pgadmin-4-critical-authorization-bypass-and-rce/

TanStack Npm Packages Compromised Inside The Mini Shai Hulud Supply Chain Attack

Snyk
2026-05-11 12 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On May 11, 2026, the Mini Shai-Hulud worm compromised 84 npm package artifacts across 42 @tanstack/* packages (as well as @squawk/*, @mistralai/* packages, and others) by chaining a GitHub Actions "Pwn Request," cache poisoning, and OIDC token extraction from runner memory — producing the first npm supply chain attack with valid SLSA Build Level 3 attestations. Here's what happened, what was stolen, and what you need to do right now.

[LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud Wave 4 (TanStack/TeamPCP) worm payload file created in node_modules Installation High
Hunts the smuggled payload artifacts (router_init.js, tanstack_runner.js, vite_setup.mjs) that the May 11 2026 TanStack supply chain attack injected into compromised npm tarballs. These filenames are not declared in any legitimate package.json `files` field, so any FileCreated event for them inside a node_modules path is high-fidelity evidence of an affected install. Rationale: router_init.js / tanstack_runner.js / vite_setup.mjs are explicitly named in the Snyk article as smuggled tarball artifacts and the prepare-hook target (`bun run tanstack_runner.js && exit 1`). They are not in any legitimate TanStack source tree, so a file-creation event under node_modules is a true-positive indicator. Hashes ab4fc...266c and 2ec78d...fc96 are the file SHA256s extracted for this campaign; the master-key hash 0c0e87...da was deliberately excluded (it is a PBKDF2 key, not a file hash). Cross-referenced against prior-session corroboration of the TeamPCP campaign family (mem-obs 305, 317-322) and OSSF MAL-2026-3432 / GHSA-g7cv-rxg3-hmpx. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g7cv-rxg3-hmpx • https://security.snyk.io/ • https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages (MAL-2026-3432)

[LLM] Session/Oxen P2P exfil DNS or TCP to getsession.org from build/CI host Command & Control High
Hunts the Wave 4 worm's exfiltration channel: encrypted upload to filev2.getsession.org plus seed{1,2,3}.getsession.org Session network nodes. This P2P messenger infrastructure has no legitimate use in CI runners or developer build hosts, and the campaign uses it precisely because IP-blocking is ineffective — DNS is the practical perimeter control. Rationale: filev2.getsession.org and seed{1,2,3}.getsession.org are explicitly named in the Snyk article as the Wave 4 exfil endpoints, with the author noting *.getsession.org DNS-level blocking is the practical perimeter control. Session is a niche P2P messenger; legitimate enterprise CI/build traffic to these domains is effectively zero, giving very high fidelity. Cross-checked against prior-session corroboration of the TeamPCP campaign (mem-obs 305, 317-322) which confirms shared exfil patterns across the Bitwarden CLI / SAP / TanStack waves. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g7cv-rxg3-hmpx • https://security.snyk.io/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog (TeamPCP attribution)

  messenger network used by the Wave 4 Mini Shai-Hulud (TanStack/TeamPCP) worm

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Talos weekly prevalent-malware hash match (Coinminer / Injector / Dropper.Miner) Installation High
Sweep endpoint process, file-write and image-load telemetry for any of the five SHA256s published in the 2026-05-07 Talos Threat Source newsletter as the most prevalent malware files (Win.Worm.Coinminer, W32.Injector, Auto.90B145, MalwareXgenMisc, Win.Dropper.Miner). High-confidence retro-hunt and forward-looking alert because Talos has already attributed each hash to a known family. Rationale: Five SHA256s plus the matching MD5s come straight from the Talos newsletter's 'Most prevalent malware files' block, each with a Talos detection name (Win.Worm.Coinminer::1201, W32.Injector:Gen.21ie.1201, Auto.90B145.282358.in02, W32.Variant:MalwareXgenMisc.29d4.1201, Win.Dropper.Miner::95.sbx.tg). Hashes are non-ambiguous primary IOCs - matching them across process/file/image-load gives an alerting-tier signal with effectively zero false positives. Did not need external corroboration; Talos publishes both the hash and the family name itself.

[LLM] Talos dropper filename pattern d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_<N>_Exe.exe Installation Medium
Hunts processes or file writes whose name matches the very distinctive Talos-observed dropper naming scheme '<MD5-of-parent>_<sequential int>_Exe.exe' - specifically the d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274 family that produced both the W32.Injector (_63_Exe.exe) and Win.Dropper.Miner (_62_Exe.exe) variants in the 2026-05-07 prevalence list. Catches as-yet-unseen sequence numbers (e.g. _64_, _65_) of the same campaign even when a fresh sample's hash hasn't propagated to threat intel yet. Rationale: Both Talos sample filenames d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_62_Exe.exe (a31f222f...) and d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_63_Exe.exe (96fa6a77...) share the same 32-hex-prefix + sequential integer + _Exe.exe suffix - this is a unique enough pattern to act as a hunting anchor for sibling samples whose hashes haven't yet been published. The leading hex string is itself the MD5 of an unspecified parent file, and the _Exe.exe (capital E) suffix is highly atypical for benign software. Marked hunting-tier rather than alerting because we have only two confirmed sequence numbers and want analyst review before auto-blocking new ones.
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let DropperPattern = @"(?i)^d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_\d+_Exe\.exe$";
union isfuzzy=true
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName matches regex DropperPattern
  | extend Seq = toint(extract(@"_(\d+)_Exe\.exe$", 1, FileName))
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, Seq, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, Source="ProcessEvents"),
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
  | where FileName matches regex DropperPattern
  | extend Seq = toint(extract(@"_(\d+)_Exe\.exe$", 1, FileName))
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, Seq, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="FileEvents")
| order by Timestamp desc
let DropperPattern = @"(?i)d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_\d+_Exe\.exe$";
union isfuzzy=true
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where TargetProcessName matches regex DropperPattern
  | extend Seq = toint(extract(@"_(\d+)_Exe\.exe$", 1, TargetProcessName))
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, Seq, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5, Source="ImProcessCreate"),
(SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where NewProcessName matches regex DropperPattern
  | extend Seq = toint(extract(@"_(\d+)_Exe\.exe$", 1, NewProcessName))
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, Seq, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source="SecurityEvent_4688"),
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
  | where TargetFileName matches regex DropperPattern
  | extend Seq = toint(extract(@"_(\d+)_Exe\.exe$", 1, TargetFileName))
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, Seq, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileMD5, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImFileEvent")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Talos Dropper Filename Pattern d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_<N>_Exe.exe
